# Intuit (INTU) — A Deep Dive on Management and the Setup

*Forensic dossier from six consecutive earnings calls (Q3 FY2025 through Q3 FY2026, May 2025–May 2026), cross-referenced against the screener's hard financials. Prepared for the investment committee. Live price used: $274.96 (NASDAQ, USD), roughly 66% below the 52-week high of $813.70.*

---

## 1. Narrative Arc

Across these six quarters the story never changed its destination, only its weather. From the very first call (Q3 FY2025, May 2025) management framed Intuit as an "AI-driven expert platform" whose edge is the fusion of proprietary data, domain-specific AI, and AI-enabled human experts ("HI"). That framing hardened over the year into a single thesis repeated almost verbatim every quarter: customers "buy confidence, not code," and in a regulated, high-stakes financial world they will keep paying humans-plus-machines even as raw software gets cheaper.

Three growth engines were introduced early and pushed harder each quarter: (1) **mid-market**, via Intuit Enterprise Suite (IES), a new AI-native ERP for $2.5M–$100M-revenue businesses inside an ~$89–90B addressable market; (2) the **"virtual team of AI agents"** (accounting, payments, payroll, tax agents) launched July 2025 and scaled to over 3 million users with 85%+ repeat engagement by Q2 FY2026; and (3) the **money/payments portfolio** (payments volume +29–30%, Bill Pay volume nearly doubling). Two large partnerships — with OpenAI (Intuit apps inside ChatGPT) and Anthropic (Claude capabilities inside IES) — were added to the narrative in late 2025.

The one genuine narrative contraction is in **consumer/DIY tax**. Early calls celebrated "breakthrough" TurboTax Live growth (+47% in FY2025). By Q3 FY2026 (May 2026) the CEO turned unusually candid: "I'm constructively dissatisfied… We faced pressure among the most price-sensitive DIY filers earning less than $50,000 a year. We lost on price." That is the admission that broke the stock. Separately, **Mailchimp** quietly slid from "get it back to growth" (Aug 2025) to "all options are on the table" and running it "for profitability" like the declining desktop business (Feb–May 2026) — a soft signal of a possible divestiture or wind-down.

## 2. Claims vs Financials (forensic)

| Management claim | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Double-digit revenue growth with margin expansion" | FY25 revenue +15.6% to $18.83B; gross margin 80.8% (expanding); net margin 20.5%; Q1/Q2/Q3 FY26 revenue +18%/+17%/+10% | Verified — though Q3 FY26 decelerated to +10% on the tax-season DIY miss |
| "Operating income grows faster than revenue" | FY25 non-GAAP operating income +18% vs revenue +16%; TTM return on equity 23.3%, return on invested capital 16.2% (both up from the FY ROE 16.6%/ROIC 12.3% in the scan) | Verified — returns are rising, not falling |
| Strong, durable free cash flow | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow $7.71B; free-cash-flow yield ~10.3%; earnings beat 7 of 7 quarters | Verified, with one important caveat below |
| "ARPC growth and margin expansion" from AI + human experts | EPS $13.67 FY25 (+31%); TTM diluted EPS $16.50; consensus forward EPS growth +15% | Verified |
| Mid-market is the big engine | IES/QBO-Advanced online ecosystem revenue +40%/+40%/+38% in Q1/Q2/Q3 FY26; IES contracts +~50% then +37% quarter-on-quarter | Verified — the crown jewel is real and accelerating |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers:** reported free cash flow flatters the owner's true return. Stock-based compensation runs at ~9.7% of revenue (~$1.9B a year, roughly a quarter of that $7.71B free-cash-flow figure). Two of the screener's deep-value models — earnings-power value and owner-earnings — show *negative* margin of safety (the stock looks fully-to-over-valued once you strip growth credit and charge for that dilution), even as the Graham and 15%-grower models show large discounts. The 17% workforce reduction announced in mid-2026 is explicitly aimed at curbing this dilution — an implicit acknowledgment that the compensation drag was real.

**Where the story is poorer than the numbers deserve:** the market has priced the whole franchise as if the DIY-tax crack were the whole company. DIY is only the ~$5B-addressable, price-sensitive slice of TurboTax; assisted tax (TurboTax Live, +36% revenue, now over half of TurboTax), mid-market, and the money portfolio are all growing north of 30%. The tape (down ~66% from the high) is far more bearish than a mid-teens-growth, 80%-gross-margin, roughly net-cash compounder warrants.

## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with a late, honest defensive turn.** Management's tone was uniformly offensive and specific through late 2025 — raising guidance "across all total company metrics" (Q3 FY25), citing hard adoption stats (2.8M then 3M+ agent users; 237M transactions categorized in a single month). The confidence never became evasive, but by Q3 FY2026 the register shifted from pure offense to candid defense: "constructively dissatisfied," "we lost on price," and a plan to "evolve our DIY business model." The CFO layered in cost-discipline language (running Mailchimp and desktop "for profitability," headcount optimization, developers "coding up to 40% faster"). This is the language of a management team that met an unexpected headwind and is reallocating rather than hiding.

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**Reliability: High.** The screener records a 7-for-7 (100%) earnings-beat rate, and the qualitative record matches: guidance was raised in Q3 FY25, delivered as promised in Q4 FY25 (full-year revenue +16%, "more than a 2-point acceleration"), and raised again in Q3 FY26 for full-year revenue and all non-GAAP metrics even while absorbing the DIY shortfall. The one blemish is a genuine forecasting miss on DIY unit growth for the 2026 tax season — but management flagged an industry-wide contraction (total IRS filers down ~30 basis points, "the most significant industry-wide contraction since the post-COVID season"), which is verifiable macro context rather than an excuse manufactured after the fact. There is a mild, healthy sandbag pattern (assisted-tax and mid-market repeatedly beat their own "15–20%" long-term framing).

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

Analysts pushed hardest, and repeatedly, on two fronts. First, **AI disintermediation**: Evercore's Kirk Materne (Q3 FY26) asked directly why more powerful models won't "disintermediate the strength you're seeing in the assisted category," and Goldman's Gabriela Borges probed where general tools like Claude Cowork stop and Intuit's domain moat begins. Management's answer was consistent and, on the evidence, credible: the ~$300B addressable market is >50% human-expert spend, that mix "structurally has not changed in 10 years," and Intuit is embedding third-party models as "context" while its own domain models remain "core." Second, **Mailchimp** — Jefferies' Brent Thill pressed on the path back to growth in three consecutive calls; the answer decayed from "a couple of quarters" to "all options on the table," which analysts correctly read as a coming portfolio decision. The DIY-tax weakness that ultimately hit the stock was *not* something analysts pre-empted — it arrived in the Q3 FY26 print itself.

## 6. Red Flags / Green Flags

🔴 The DIY-filer price loss is a real, dated crack in the consumer moat — the first segment where "good-enough" cheaper alternatives visibly won on price (Q3 FY26).
🔴 Securities-fraud investigations and class-action filings (BFA Law, Pomerantz, Robbins LLP; class period Aug 22 2025–May 20 2026) followed the ~20% post-earnings drop — headline and litigation overhang, though such suits rarely impair a franchise of this quality.
🔴 Stock-based compensation at ~9.7% of revenue meaningfully inflates the headline free-cash-flow yield; owner-earnings and earnings-power-value models see no discount.
🔴 Mailchimp's drift from "return to growth" to "run for cash / all options open" is an admission that a large 2021-era acquisition underperformed.
🟢 Mid-market (IES) is accelerating, not fading — online ecosystem revenue for QBO-Advanced/IES grew ~40% for three straight quarters, with accountant-channel partnerships compounding a network effect.
🟢 Margins and returns are expanding through the drawdown — TTM return on equity 23.3%, return on invested capital 16.2%, gross margin ~81%.
🟢 Management is returning capital aggressively into the sell-off — an ~$8B repurchase authorization plus the cost-out program, buying stock at ~10x forward earnings.
🟢 OpenAI and Anthropic partnerships convert the feared disruptors into distribution — Intuit's apps run *inside* ChatGPT while it keeps "the economics we enjoy today."

## 7. Hidden Signals

The most telling terminology shift is the reframing of AI from threat to distribution. Early calls sold AI as internal productivity; by Q2–Q3 FY2026 the CEO reframed the very models investors feared as Intuit's own funnel: partnering with OpenAI/Anthropic to "be where the eyeballs are," treating Claude as "context" that Intuit's domain models orchestrate. The CFO's crisp "office of the CFO/COO/CEO is core to us; the shipping department is context" is a deliberate moat-boundary statement aimed straight at the disintermediation bears. A second signal: the repeated, almost insistent invocation of "regulated environment," "liability," "accuracy," "compliance" — management has clearly decided the durable defense is *trust and accountability*, not features. Third, an investor-relations reshuffle (long-time IR head Kim Watkins departing, a senior strategic-finance SVP taking over IR) coincides with the more disciplined capital-allocation and cost language — consistent with a company girding for a re-rating fight.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE (a strengthening core carrying one eroding sub-segment through an AI-fear drawdown).** The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is a genuine wide-moat compounder priced as a melting asset, but the bear case rests on a *real* secular force — that generative AI collapses the price of "good-enough" tax and bookkeeping — and that force has already drawn first blood in DIY tax. The committee must judge whether the DIY crack is contained to the smallest, most price-sensitive slice (the financials and the >30%-growth of every other engine say yes) or the leading edge of a broader commoditization (the ~66% de-rating says the market fears the latter).

**Moat:** switching-costs + regulatory-trust + data-scale + accountant network effect — genuinely **wide**. The evidence base is a rising return on invested capital (16.2% trailing), expanding ~81% gross margin, and 85%+ agent-repeat engagement — a widening, not eroding, economic engine on the numbers. **Moat trend: stable** (widening on mid-market and margin; tested at the DIY edge). **Secular threat: material, not terminal** — AI-displacement is real and has impaired one segment's pricing, but Intuit is so far adapting (embedding the disruptors as distribution, growing the assisted/expert TAM that AI *cannot* easily serve) rather than being disintermediated. The cheapness reads as a fear-print in a rotation out of former winners, not (yet) a structurally-shrinking base — but the thesis lives or dies on whether QuickBooks bookkeeping resists the same price collapse that hit DIY tax.

What broke on 20 May 2026 was this: third-quarter revenue growth halved to 10%, the company cut its full-year TurboTax revenue outlook to $5.277 billion, announced a 17% workforce reduction of roughly 3,000 roles, and chief executive Sasan Goodarzi admitted 'We lost on price' among do-it-yourself filers earning under $50,000. The shares fell 20% the next day to $307.07.

Here is what that admission actually covers. The do-it-yourself tier is a $5 billion market — 12% of TurboTax's addressable base. The other 88%, where people pay someone else to do the work, grew 36% this year. TurboTax Live is now over half of TurboTax revenue, up 11 points year-over-year. So the segment the market believes is dying is, in its large majority, accelerating. And the loss happened in a season when total filings across the whole industry shrank by about 30 basis points — roughly 2 million returns, the worst contraction since the post-COVID season. Intuit lost the cheap end of a shrinking pool and chose not to buy it back with price.

Meanwhile the actual engine of the company is compounding. Global Business Solutions — QuickBooks, payroll, payments, the mid-market suite — is 59% of revenue at roughly $12.8 billion and growing about 15%. Inside it, the mid-market push into a ~$90 billion opportunity grew roughly 38-40% for three straight quarters, with Intuit Enterprise Suite contracts up about 50% quarter-over-quarter in the second quarter and 37% in the third. Payments volume grew 30%. The money portfolio grew 26%. Return on invested capital is about 16.2% trailing, up from 12.3% on the last full fiscal year. Return on equity is 23.3%. The crack is real and it is reported fact, not fear: Intuit lost price-sensitive filers to cheaper competitors and cut its tax guidance. The bear case is simply that this is the leading edge of the bite, not the trailing edge.

The sequence is what should worry a buyer. In February 2026 management declared 'We are a category of one' and told Goldman Sachs's Gabriela Borges that the market structure favouring human experts 'structurally has not changed in the last 10 years. It hasn't changed in the last 6 months.' Three months later the company lost the low end on price and fired 3,000 people. Either management did not know its own competitive position, or it did. Both readings are bad, and a securities class action now covers precisely that window — purchasers between 22 August 2025 and 20 May 2026, filed in the Northern District of California under docket 26-cv-07086, with a lead-plaintiff deadline of 8 September 2026. The analyst who probed the moat hardest, Borges, downgraded the stock to a sell rating on 2 June 2026 at a $276 target. Piper Sandler set a $250 target on 14 July 2026 — below where the stock trades today.

Latest-quarter earnings per share grew 11% year-over-year against a three-year compound rate of 23.4%. Credit Karma decelerated from 32% growth in fiscal 2025 to 15% in the third quarter.
